blocks.text: FloppyData in 2026: what you get

FloppyData sells proxies the way prepaid phone plans sell minutes: one flat $1/GB balance that works across residential, mobile and datacenter pools. Static residential IPs start at $1.79 each in monthly bundles (20 for $49) with unlimited bandwidth. It is one of the cheapest ways into residential traffic, but it is a newer brand with less independent benchmarking than the established names.

Strengths: Flat $1/GB on any volume; One balance across residential, mobile and datacenter; Cheap static residential bundles with unlimited bandwidth; Free cloud anti-detect browser. Weak spots: Newer brand with limited independent testing; Pool-size claims disputed by some reviewers; Mixed customer-support reviews.
ProxyEmpire in 2026: what you get

ProxyEmpire sells residential, mobile, static residential and datacenter proxies from one dashboard and competes on flexibility. Traffic you prepay never expires, ISP-level targeting is free, and the $1.97 trial lets you test both residential and mobile networks before committing. Its 30M+ advertised pool is smaller on paper than the enterprise providers, but independent testing has rated its real reachable pool well relative to its claims.

Strengths: Prepaid traffic rolls over indefinitely; ISP/ASN targeting included at no extra cost; Cheap $1.97 trial covering residential and mobile; Unlimited residential option priced per day. Weak spots: Smaller advertised pool than the big three; Exact GB thresholds for each tier only shown at checkout; Weaker results on Google in some independent tests.
Pricing: FloppyData vs ProxyEmpire

FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB for rotating traffic, and the same balance works for residential, mobile and datacenter IPs. Static residential proxies are sold in monthly bundles from $1.79 per IP (20 IPs for $49), and static datacenter IPs from $0.79 per IP.

ProxyEmpire's rotating residential pricing currently starts at $3.50/GB (shown as 50% off a $7 list price) and steps down through several tiers to $1.50/GB at 1 TB, with custom pricing from about $0.75/GB above 5 TB. Rotating mobile starts at $4.50/GB, rotating datacenter at about $0.65/GB, and a flat-rate unlimited residential plan is sold by the day.

For a 10 GB month, FloppyData costs about $10 while ProxyEmpire costs about $35, so FloppyData saves around 71%. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because ProxyEmpire does not publish an exact price for that volume; FloppyData comes to about $100. Look past the per-GB figure too. ProxyEmpire lets unused traffic carry forward, while FloppyData's allowance does not (check current terms). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

FloppyData does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. FloppyData lists '65M+ claimed (disputed)' and ProxyEmpire lists '30M+'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, FloppyData lists 148 (residential) countries and ProxyEmpire lists 170+. On targeting, FloppyData offers country and city, while ProxyEmpire offers country, region, city and ISP/ASN (included by default).
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, FloppyData offers rotating or sticky sessions, and ProxyEmpire offers rotating or sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?
General web scraping: ProxyEmpire. ProxyEmpire has the edge here. Why: stable connections and traffic that never expires. How FloppyData compares: cheap, but with limited independent benchmarking.

SERP and rank tracking: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. FloppyData: workable for light tasks. ProxyEmpire: Google was its weakest target in independent tests. Let price and the countries you need decide.

Social media and multi-account management: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. FloppyData: cheap static residential IPs and a free anti-detect browser. ProxyEmpire: residential and mobile IPs with 24-hour sticky sessions. Let price and the countries you need decide.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: ProxyEmpire. ProxyEmpire has the edge here. Why: free city and ISP targeting. How FloppyData compares: city targeting at a flat rate.
Ad verification and geo-testing: ProxyEmpire. ProxyEmpire has the edge here. Why: ISP-level targeting at no extra cost. How FloppyData compares: limited targeting depth and published data.
Tight budgets: FloppyData wins. The deciding factor for FloppyData: a flat $1/GB on any volume. The limitation on the ProxyEmpire side: rollover means nothing you pay for is wasted.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. FloppyData: No free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations. ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile. Verification and payment rules differ too. FloppyData: Light. ProxyEmpire: Standard verification. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test FloppyData and ProxyEmpire before you commit
The quickest way to choose between FloppyData and ProxyEmpire is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (FloppyData: no free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations; ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, FloppyData comes out ahead in 1, ProxyEmpire in 3, and 2 are ties. That makes ProxyEmpire the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: FloppyData is strongest for small budgets and experiments, while ProxyEmpire is strongest for teams that hate losing unused bandwidth. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
